questions.text:
Let [latex]M[/latex] be a nondeterministic finite automaton (NFA) with [latex]6[/latex] states over a finite alphabet.
Which of the following options CANNOT be the number of states in the minimal deterministic finite automaton (DFA) that is equivalent to [latex]M[/latex] ?
questions.solution:
By the subset construction, any [latex]n[/latex]-state NFA has an equivalent DFA with at most [latex]2^n[/latex] states (one state for every subset of NFA states), and the minimal DFA has at most that many states as well (minimization can only reduce, never increase, the state count).

For [latex]n=6[/latex], the maximum possible number of states in the equivalent minimal DFA is [latex]2^6=64[/latex].

- [latex]32\le64[/latex]: achievable.
- [latex]1\le64[/latex]: achievable (e.g. an NFA accepting all strings can minimize to a single-state DFA).
- [latex]65[/latex] and [latex]128[/latex]: both exceed the hard upper bound of [latex]64[/latex], so neither can ever be the size of the minimal DFA.

Answer: 65 and 128 CANNOT be the number of states.

questions.text:
Consider the following C statements:

char *str1 = "Hello; /* Statement S1 */
char *str2 = "Hello;"; /* Statement S2 */
int *str3 = "Hello"; /* Statement S3 */

Which of the following options is/are correct?
questions.solution:
[latex]\text{S1: char *str1 = "Hello;}[/latex] — the string literal is missing its closing double-quote. An unterminated string literal is a lexical error (the lexer/scanner cannot even form a valid string token).

[latex]\text{S2: char *str2 = "Hello;";}[/latex] — this is a perfectly valid string literal (containing a semicolon character) assigned to a [latex]\text{char *}[/latex]; no error at all.

[latex]\text{S3: int *str3 = "Hello";}[/latex] — this is lexically and syntactically fine (a valid string literal, valid statement syntax), but it assigns a [latex]\text{char *}[/latex] value to an incompatible [latex]\text{int *}[/latex] pointer type. This is a type-mismatch, which is a semantic error (caught during semantic/type analysis, not parsing).

Answer: S1 has a lexical error, and S3 has a semantic error.

options: [latex]\text{S2}[/latex] has a lexical error and [latex]\text{S3}[/latex] has a syntactic error
[latex]\text{S1}[/latex] has a lexical error and [latex]\text{S3}[/latex] has a semantic error
[latex]\text{S1}[/latex] has a syntactic error and [latex]\text{S3}[/latex] has a semantic error

questions.text: Which of the following statements is/are true?
questions.solution:
Checking each claim about LL(1) parsing:

- "LL(1) parser uses backtracking" — false. LL(1) is a predictive, backtrack-free top-down parser: it decides the production to use by looking at only one lookahead symbol.
- "For LL(1), the grammar must be left-recursive" — false, in fact the opposite: a left-recursive grammar can never be LL(1) (it would cause infinite recursion in the predictive parser), so left recursion must first be eliminated.
- "For LL(1), the grammar must be left-factored" — true. If two productions of a non-terminal share a common prefix, the parser cannot decide which one to use from one lookahead symbol; left-factoring removes this ambiguity, which is a necessary step towards making a grammar LL(1).
- "LL(1) parsers are more powerful than SLR parsers" — false. LL(1) and SLR(1) are different (incomparable) classes of grammars; SLR(1), being bottom-up, actually accepts a strictly larger class of grammars than LL(1) in general, so LL(1) is not "more powerful."

Answer: For a grammar to be LL(1), it must be left-factored.

For a grammar to be [latex]\text{LL(1)}[/latex], it must be left-factored

questions.text: With respect to deadlocks in an operating system, which of the following statements is/are FALSE?
questions.solution:
Evaluating each deadlock-related statement:

- "Banker's algorithm is used to prevent deadlocks" — FALSE. Banker's algorithm is a deadlock-avoidance algorithm (it checks resource requests dynamically to keep the system in a safe state); deadlock prevention refers to a different set of techniques that structurally rule out one of the four necessary conditions (mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no pre-emption, circular wait).
- "Deadlock formation can be prevented by disallowing hold-and-wait" — true: this is a standard, valid deadlock-prevention technique (one of the four necessary conditions is removed).
- "An assignment edge in a resource-allocation graph is marked from a process to a resource" — FALSE. It's the reverse: an assignment edge goes from a resource to a process (resource is allocated to the process); a request edge goes from a process to a resource.
- "A safe state guarantees all processes can finish without deadlock" — true: this is precisely the definition of a safe state.

Answer (the FALSE statements): "Banker's algorithm prevents deadlocks", and "an assignment edge goes from process to resource."

options: Banker's algorithm is used to prevent deadlocks
Deadlock formation can be prevented by ensuring that the hold and wait condition is not allowed
An assignment edge in a resource allocation graph is marked from a process to a resource
A safe state guarantees that all processes can finish without formation of a deadlock

questions.text:
Let [latex]P, Q, R[/latex] and [latex]S[/latex] be the attributes of a relation in a relational schema. Let [latex]X \rightarrow Y[/latex] indicate functional dependency in the context of a relational database, where [latex]X, Y \subseteq\{P, Q, R, S\}[/latex].

Which of the following options is/are always true?
questions.solution:
Using Armstrong's axioms (reflexivity, augmentation, transitivity) to test each claim:

- {P,Q}→{R} and {P}→{R}, does {Q}→{R} follow? No — {P}→{R} already implies {P,Q}→{R} by augmentation, so the premises give no information forcing {Q}→{R} to hold. Not always true.
- {P,Q}→{R}, does {P}→{R} or {Q}→{R} follow? No — {R} may genuinely require both P and Q together (e.g. R functionally depends on the pair but on neither attribute alone). Not always true.
- {P}→{R} and {Q}→{S}, does {P,Q}→{R,S} follow? Yes: augment {P}→{R} with Q to get {P,Q}→{R,Q}; augment {Q}→{S} with P to get {P,Q}→{P,S}; using reflexivity ({R,Q}→{R} and {P,S}→{S}) and transitivity gives {P,Q}→{R} and {P,Q}→{S}; the union rule then gives {P,Q}→{R,S}. Always true.
- {P}→{R}, does {P,Q}→{R} follow? Yes, directly by the augmentation axiom (adding Q to the left-hand side of a valid FD keeps it valid). Always true.

Answer: {P}→{R},{Q}→{S} &there4 {P,Q}→{R,S}; and {P}→{R} &there4 {P,Q}→{R}.
